title: The Tide of Rosewater Lane
premise: Felix Marchetti has spent ten years exchanging anonymous letters with a stranger who signed only 'W,' the one relationship she never tried to control—until the letters stopped two years ago and she convinced herself it was a mercy. When Wren Ashford, a disgraced former prosecutor turned small-town restorer of an old seaside inn, moves into the house next door, Felix recognizes the handwriting on the moving boxes and realizes her correspondent has been closer than she ever imagined. As Felix investigates the corruption case that destroyed Wren's career, she discovers the truth implicates her own late grandfather's lighthouse records, and that staying invisible means letting an innocent person fall. When Wren's enemies arrive to finish what they started, Felix must choose between the safety of her contained heart and testifying to what she knows—ending with Wren cleared, the lighthouse relit, and Felix finally letting someone stay past the last train.
about_author: Juniper Vane is the pen name of a former coastal archivist who spent seven years cataloguing lighthouse keeper logs along the Atlantic seaboard. She writes romance for readers who believe love is less a lightning strike than a tide—patient, insistent, and impossible to argue with.

chapters.title: The Muscle of the Heart
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. On the first anniversary of the last letter, Felix catalogs her ordered life: the lighthouse cottage, her half-finished novel, her rule against permanence. A flashback shows her grandfather teaching her that everything the sea takes can be tracked. Emotional beat: controlled loneliness presented as freedom.

chapters.title: Letters to W
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. She rereads a decade of correspondence, tracing how 'W' knew things about her no one else did—including her mother's disappearance. The final letter, two years old, said only 'I have to stop before I ruin this.' Beat: longing disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: The Moving Van on Rosewater Lane
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A stranger arrives at the derelict Harrow Inn next door: Wren Ashford, buying the property outright with city money and a closed expression. Felix notices the distinctive slanted handwriting on the boxes. Beat: the floor drops out of her certainty.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren has come to the coast to disappear after a corruption scandal ended her prosecutor career, carrying guilt over a case she was forced to bury. She recognizes her neighbor's name from ten years of letters and panics. Beat: dread braided with hope.

chapters.title: Borrowed Sugar, Borrowed Time
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A deliberately casual first conversation at the fence line; Felix tests Wren with an oblique reference to the letters and watches her flinch. Neither confesses. Beat: two people fencing with politeness.

chapters.title: The Inn's Bones
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Restoring the inn, Wren finds a hidden cache in the wall: lighthouse logs from Felix's grandfather, documenting ship movements that don't match official records. Beat: the first thread of the larger mystery.

chapters.title: What the Logs Say
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Wren shows Felix the logs; Felix recognizes her grandfather's hand noting unlogged cargo runs—evidence of smuggling someone protected. Beat: her family's clean legacy cracks.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Flashback chapter: how the letters began when Felix, nineteen and grieving, mailed a complaint to the district attorney's office and a junior prosecutor answered personally. Beat: tenderness for her younger self.

chapters.title: The Case That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren explains in interior monologue why she stopped writing: she discovered her own office was compromised, and staying close to Felix put her in danger. Beat: protective sacrifice revealed to the reader, hidden from Felix.

chapters.title: Last Train at 9:40
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Town texture chapter: the last evening train, the stationmaster's warning that the line closes for good in three months, cutting the town off. The ticking clock is established. Beat: quiet dread.

chapters.title: An Invitation, Grudging
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A storm knocks out the inn's power; Felix grudgingly shelters Wren overnight. They talk until dawn about everything except the letters. Beat: intimacy breaking through armor.

chapters.title: The Man from the Harbor Trust
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A smooth stranger, Callum Reeve, arrives claiming to audit the inn's purchase—Wren recognizes him as the fixer who buried her case. Beat: the past arrives wearing a smile.

chapters.title: Research Is a Love Language
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix, novelist's instinct sharpening, starts pulling harbor records at the library, mapping her grandfather's logs against Reeve's family's shipping company. Beat: purpose replacing paralysis.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A near-kiss on the inn's half-built porch interrupted by Reeve's car. Wren retreats, still protecting Felix by withholding. Beat: frustration and ache.

chapters.title: The Penmanship Problem
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix compares the inn's permit signatures to her letters—same hand. She confronts Wren, who admits to being 'W' but lies about why she stopped. Beat: betrayal inside vindication.

chapters.title: Cold Shoulder, Warm House
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Felix cuts Wren off; Wren throws herself into the restoration, leaving the porch light on every night as a silent apology. Beat: stubborn hearts talking through architecture.

chapters.title: Grandfather's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. In the attic, Felix finds her grandfather's final log, dated days before his death, naming the ship, the cargo—and initials that match Reeve's father. Beat: grief and fury fusing into resolve.

chapters.title: The Accident Question
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reveals to the reader (not Felix) that her buried case involved the same shipping company, and that a witness died. She begins to suspect the lighthouse keeper's death wasn't accidental. Beat: horror compounding.

chapters.title: Truce at the Lighthouse
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix, needing Wren's legal knowledge, proposes a cold alliance: truth for truth. Wren tells her everything about the buried case—except her feelings. Beat: partnership with a wall down the middle.

chapters.title: What the Harbor Remembers
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The pair interviews old fishermen; one, drunk and frightened, confirms the night runs and says Reeve's men 'handled' the keeper. Beat: the stakes turn mortal.

chapters.title: The Fisherman Who Talked
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The witness recants after a visit from Reeve, then disappears. Wren's guilt over her old case's dead witness doubles. Beat: the cost of silence made personal.

chapters.title: Felix Writes a Chapter
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix drafts her novel's ending and realizes she's been writing Wren all along—the anonymous correspondent was her muse and her cowardice both. Beat: self-recognition.

chapters.title: Reeve Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Reeve offers Wren her career back if she hands over the logs and leaves town. Wren pretends to consider. Beat: temptation as reconnaissance.

chapters.title: The Night Visitor
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Someone breaks into the cottage searching for the logs; Felix hides them in the lighthouse and realizes she's being watched. Wren arrives too late, and Felix, shaken, lets her stay the night. Beat: fear dissolving the last wall.

chapters.title: Say It Plainly
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. At dawn, the truth finally lands: they confess both the decade of letters and the love underneath them. One perfect day before the storm. Beat: earned tenderness, deliberately placed before catastrophe.

chapters.title: The Line Closes
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The last train departs for good; the town is now reachable only by road that Reeve's company is buying. Felix watches the tracks empty and understands there is no leaving anymore. Beat: the escape route dies.

chapters.title: Paper Trails
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren drafts a whistleblower complaint using the logs, the fisherman's earlier statement, and Felix's research, but needs the original harbor master's ledger—held in the county archive Reeve controls. Beat: the plan's impossible middle.

chapters.title: The Archive Job
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A tense, quiet caper chapter: Felix uses her archivist skills and a borrowed badge to photograph the ledger while Wren distracts the clerk—Reeve himself. Beat: competence and terror in equal measure.

chapters.title: Caught
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Reeve confronts Wren with security footage; he gives her until Friday to hand over everything or he'll prosecute Felix for theft and reveal Wren's role in the old cover-up. Beat: the trap closes on both of them.

chapters.title: The Containable Heart Fails
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix, ready to confess and take the fall alone, finds Wren has already signed a false statement taking all blame. Furious, Felix burns her own rulebook: she calls the one journalist who owes her grandfather's memory. Beat: love as refusal to be protected.

chapters.title: Friday
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The deadline day: Reeve arrives at the inn with an attorney and a sheriff's deputy; the town gathers; the journalist's article publishes online mid-standoff. Beat: everything converging.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse Speaks
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Climax. Felix leads the crowd to the lighthouse, relights the lamp her grandfather kept, and projects the evidence—logs, ledger photos, the dead witness's letter—into public view as the beam sweeps the harbor. Reeve's men are recognized by the fishermen he wronged. Beat: justice outside the law, witnessed by a whole town.

chapters.title: Aftermath in the Rain
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Reeve is arrested by state investigators; Wren faces her own reckoning for the cover-up she was coerced into, offering to testify fully. Beat: accountability as redemption.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Wren accepts a suspended sentence and disbarment rather than a deal that silences her. Felix waits at the courthouse steps—not to fix it, but to be there. Beat: love without rescue.

chapters.title: What Stays
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Quiet chapter: winter settles, the inn's first rooms open, Felix finishes her novel and dedicates it 'to W, wherever you were.' Beat: softness after storm.

chapters.title: The Unsent Letter
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren writes Felix a real, signed letter—ten years of things she couldn't say—and leaves it in the lighthouse where Felix will find it. Beat: vulnerability without armor.

chapters.title: Reading by Lamplight
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix reads the letter in the lamp room as dawn comes, and for the first time doesn't catalog or contain what she feels. Beat: the heart, finally untrained.

chapters.title: The Question at the Fence
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Spring. Wren asks, plainly, to stay—not forever, just past the next season, then the next. Felix answers by handing her a key to the lighthouse. Beat: commitment without ceremony.

chapters.title: Rosewater Lane in Bloom
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The town, the inn, the relit lighthouse; Felix publishes her novel under her own name at last. Her mother's disappearance is resolved in a brief, bittersweet letter from abroad. Beat: every thread gathered.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Final chapter: the two of them on the porch as the old tracks rust quietly, no train ever coming, neither of them wanting one. Felix admits the heart was never a muscle she could train—only a tide she learned to swim in. Beat: homecoming.
